title: Session 6: Sentence Structure: Simple, Compound, Complex and Compound-Complex
summary: The four sentence structures as formulas built from IC and DC — simple, compound (three ways to join), complex (DC, IC and IC DC) and compound-complex — with the conjunctions and punctuation for each, and a lot of practice.

blocks.title: By the end of this session you can …
items: Write the formula for each of the four sentence structures
Join two ICs in the three correct ways
Build complex sentences in both orders with the right comma
Build and identify compound-complex sentences

blocks.text: You now know what an **IC** (independent clause) and a **DC** (dependent clause) are. Every sentence structure is simply a mix of them:

rows: The students finished the test, **and** the teacher collected the papers.
**When** the students finished the test, the teacher collected the papers.
**2 or more ICs + at least 1 DC**
**When** the bell rang, the students finished the test, **and** the teacher collected the papers.

items: One subject + verb pair (one clause).
It can still be long: it may have **two subjects** or **two verbs** joined by and/or/but and many phrases.
Ali and his brother **played** football in the park after school. → still simple (one clause, compound subject).
She **opened** the door and **walked** in. → still simple (one subject, two verbs, no comma).

blocks.text: 3. Compound sentence = IC + IC (three ways to join)

rows: The rain stopped, **so** we went outside.
The rain stopped**;** the sun came out.
The rain stopped**; however,** the ground was still wet.

blocks.title: Never join two ICs with …
items: **a comma only** → comma splice ✗ The rain stopped, we went outside.
**nothing at all** → run-on (fused sentence) ✗ The rain stopped we went outside.
**comma + however** → comma splice ✗ The rain stopped, however the ground was wet.

blocks.title: Use a semicolon alone only when the two ideas are closely related
items: ✓ The library was silent; everyone was studying.
✗ The library was silent; my favourite food is pizza. (no link between the ideas)

rows: **Although it was late,** we kept working.
We kept working **although it was late.**
The boy **who won the prize** is my cousin.

blocks.title: The DC can be any of the three types
items: adverb clause (because, although, when, if …) · relative clause (who, which, that …) · noun clause (that, what, why …).
I think **that** the answer is wrong. → complex (IC + noun clause).

blocks.text: Build it in steps: make a compound sentence (IC + IC), then add a DC to one of the ICs.

rows: **When the alarm rang,** I got up, **but** my brother stayed in bed.
I got up, **but** my brother stayed in bed **because he was tired.**
I got up **when the alarm rang;** **however,** my brother stayed in bed.
**Although the test was hard,** Mona finished early**;** she had revised every day.
The teacher **who marked our tests** was strict, **yet** everyone passed.

blocks.title: How to identify any sentence in 3 steps
items: 1. Find every **subject + verb** pair and count the clauses.
2. Mark each clause **IC** or **DC** (does it start with a subordinating conjunction or relative word?).
3. Use the formula: 1 IC = simple · 2+ IC = compound · IC + DC = complex · 2+ IC + DC = compound-complex.

blocks.text: 6. Review: which joining word for which structure?

rows: FANBOYS (with a comma) · semicolon · conjunctive adverbs (; however,) · correlative pairs joining two clauses (Either you … , or …)
subordinating conjunctions (although, because, when, if, until …) · relative words (who, which, that …) · that / what / why (noun clauses)

items.q: Identify: My cousin and I watched the match on TV.
Identify: My cousin watched the match, but I went to bed.
Identify: I went to bed before the match ended.
Identify: Before the match ended, I went to bed, but my cousin stayed up.
Identify: The match that we watched was exciting.
Join in three compound ways: The museum was closed. We visited the park.
items.a: …closed, so we visited the park. · …closed; we visited the park. · …closed; therefore, we visited the park.

items.q: Make it complex (DC, IC): The museum was closed. We visited the park.
items.a: Because the museum was closed, we visited the park.

items.q: Make it complex (IC DC): same sentences
items.a: We visited the park because the museum was closed.

items.q: Make it compound-complex: add a DC to The museum was closed, so we visited the park.
items.a: e.g. Because it was Friday, the museum was closed, so we visited the park.

items.q: Fix: The bus was late, we walked to school.
items.a: comma splice → The bus was late, so we walked to school. / …late; we walked…

items.q: Fix: Because the bus was late, so we walked.
items.a: Because the bus was late, we walked. (complex) / The bus was late, so we walked. (compound)

blocks.title: Session 6 Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 15 questions. Choose the best answer. You see your score and the explanations at the end.

c: 2 or more ICs + at least 1 DC

questions.q: Sara and her sister cooked and served dinner.
questions.e: one clause: compound subject + compound verb

questions.q: The phone rang, so I answered it.
Because the phone rang, I woke up.
Because the phone rang, I woke up, and I answered it.
The book that you lent me is fantastic.
Which is a correct compound sentence?
c: It was cold, however we stayed in.
It was cold we stayed in.
It was cold; we stayed in.
It was cold, we stayed in.

questions.q: Which is a correct complex sentence?
c: Although it was cold. We went out.
We went out, although, it was cold.
Although it was cold, we went out.
Although it was cold we went out.
She left early; because she was ill.
She left early because she was ill.
She left early, because, she was ill.
Because she was ill. She left early.
